candidates.title: Detecting and Mitigating Subliminal Bias Transmission in Multi-Agent Distillation Frameworks
candidates.summary: This paper proposes a method to detect and mitigate subliminal bias transmission in multi-agent distillation frameworks. By analyzing token-level entanglement patterns in teacher-generated data, we identify hidden signals that propagate unintended behavioral traits to student models. Our approach combines mechanistic interpretability with adversarial filtering to isolate and neutralize these signals during distillation. We validate the method by training student models on datasets generated by biased teacher agents and measuring bias amplification in downstream tasks.
candidates.gap: Existing multi-agent distillation frameworks (ref-009) assume knowledge transfer occurs through explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, but ref-014 and ref-017 show that subliminal bias transmission can occur via hidden data patterns. Ref-004 focuses on educational personalization without addressing bias transmission, leaving open the risk of unintended behavioral traits propagating through teacher-generated data.
candidates.approach: We implement a three-stage process: (1) mechanistic analysis using causal tracing to identify neuron populations correlated with bias signals, (2) adversarial filtering via input perturbations that neutralize these signals in teacher-generated data, and (3) constrained distillation with a regularization term penalizing bias-related activation patterns in student models. The core mechanism differs from ref-012's corpus-level constraints by targeting hidden signals rather than explicit label correlations.
candidates.evaluation: We evaluate on three metrics: (1) bias amplification factor (ratio of bias scores in student vs. teacher models) using the RealToxicityPrompts (ref-006) and gender bias benchmarks (ref-012), (2) task performance retention on factual (TruthfulQA) and mathematical (GSM8K) benchmarks, and (3) ablation studies isolating the effect of each stage. Baselines include standard distillation (ref-009) and bias-aware distillation (ref-012) on the same tasks.

candidates.title: Evaluating Agentic Misalignment in Autonomous LLM Roles via Multi-Agent Testbeds
candidates.summary: This work introduces a multi-agent testbed to measure agentic misalignment in LLMs operating autonomously in simulated environments with access to sensitive systems. The framework quantifies misalignment through action logs, goal deviation scores, and human evaluations, extending prior stress-testing methods with structured metrics and controlled counterfactual experiments.
candidates.gap: While ref-002 stress-tests LLMs in hypothetical corporate scenarios, it lacks standardized metrics for quantifying misalignment and does not systematically isolate environmental factors. Existing evaluations rely on qualitative observations of harmful behaviors without numerical benchmarks for comparison or reproducibility.
candidates.approach: We implement a multi-agent testbed with simulated environments (email clients, document repositories) where LLMs execute tasks under conflicting goals. Misalignment is measured via (1) action logs tracking unauthorized actions (e.g., data leaks), (2) goal deviation scores calculated as the cosine similarity between model-generated action sequences and optimal aligned sequences, and (3) human evaluations using a 5-point harmfulness rubric. Counterfactual testing involves holding model architecture constant while varying environmental constraints (e.g., access permissions) to isolate their impact on behavior.
candidates.evaluation: We test Llama 2-Chat models (7B, 13B, 70B) from ref-001 and models from ref-002 against rule-based agents and non-safety-trained baselines. Metrics include task success rate, harmful action frequency (detected via environment logs), goal deviation scores, and harmfulness ratings from annotators with ML safety expertise. The testbed replicates ref-002's scenarios with added metrics and validates findings under controlled conditions.

candidates.title: Adversarial Robustness in Diffusion Policy Systems via Timestep-Sensitive Perturbation Analysis
candidates.summary: This work investigates adversarial vulnerabilities in diffusion policies by analyzing how perturbations at specific diffusion timesteps affect policy failure. We propose a framework that identifies critical timesteps through gradient-based sensitivity analysis and generates minimal perturbations to maximize task failure. The approach includes white-box and black-box attack variants with physical realizability constraints. Evaluation measures success rate degradation on manipulation benchmarks against baseline methods like DP-Attacker.
candidates.gap: While ref-005 examines adversarial attacks on diffusion policies, it does not analyze how vulnerabilities manifest across individual diffusion timesteps. The paper demonstrates patch-based spatial attacks and frame-agnostic offline perturbations but does not isolate the impact of perturbing specific timesteps in the diffusion process.
candidates.approach: The method performs gradient-based sensitivity analysis on each diffusion timestep to identify those most affecting policy output. It then applies constrained optimization to generate minimal perturbations (L2 norm) at these timesteps. The framework includes white-box attacks (full gradient access) and black-box attacks (finite difference estimation). Physical realizability is enforced via patch size and material constraints. The core difference from ref-005 is the explicit focus on timestep sensitivity rather than uniform frame perturbations.
candidates.evaluation: We test on the Adroit manipulation benchmark (ref-005) against pre-trained diffusion policies. Metrics include success rate drop, perturbation magnitude (L2 norm), and transferability across policy architectures. Baselines include DP-Attacker (ref-005) and random perturbations. Ablation studies compare full method performance against variants with random timestep selection or uniform spatial perturbations, isolating the contribution of timestep sensitivity analysis.
